principles.title: Research First, Research Often
principles.body: Utilize research for identifying new opportunities and keep learning throughout a project's lifecycle using appropriate research methodologies based on project constraints, timelines, and learning objectives.

principles.title: Incremental Changes
principles.body: Design towards a future without waiting for it. Provide value to users with small improvements over time.

principles.title: Cultivate Collaboration
principles.body: Every team member's voice is valuable. Work hard to build relationships, encourage engagement from others, and bring them along for the ride.

principles.title: Consider Your Audience
principles.body: Curate communications based on who's listening. Find the right story to tell in an engaging way that is unique to your audience.

principles.title: Be Holistic
principles.body: Individual user tasks are often inter-connected. Consider the total impact across product feature teams and all platform areas when making design decisions.

principles.title: Evolve and Be Slushee
principles.body: Reflect, evaluate, and always be changing. Experiment with new processes to improve and optimize team collaboration and effectiveness.

projects.title: Customer Segmentation
projects.description: Led a customer segmentation initiative post-merger (Upright + Neatoscan) to define segments, representative customers, and needs maps, enabling better product decision-making, cohort analysis, and roadmap planning.
projects.detail: Built a scalable segmentation model for ~250 customers using a mix of quantitative “self-sorting” reports and collaborative qualitative sorting to define segment criteria, characteristics, and representative customers for feature logging and product strategy.

sections.content: Formerly competing companies, Upright Labs and Neatoscan merged in 2023. The merger kick started a product team-led investigation into the market offering across the two companies. The goal was to identify complementary and competitive features. Research into the customer base to identify themes in their structure, behavior, usage, and needs was also tasked to the product team. I led this customer segmentation project. The project involved categorizing our customers, identifying their primary needs, and evaluating the effectiveness of our total products and how well our products were meeting the needs of our customers.

projects.title: Conveyor Workflow
projects.description: Concepted a conveyor-based stationary picking workflow in Lister to speed up apparel fulfillment, reduce errors, and keep shipping cycles under one day for high-volume clothing operations.
projects.detail: Designed and documented an end-to-end stationary conveyor picking workflow for apparel orders (including bulk actions, order locking, and a cycled fulfillment screen), with assumptions, edge cases, and success metrics to support a customer pilot.

sections.content:
Select customers are interested in installing two clothing conveyors. The conveyors allow for the convent storage and picking of apparel items. Customer organizations hope to increase clothing order fulfillment efficiency with the conveyor system. The conveyor can be triggered to deliver any piece of clothing when sent a request for a given location. A picking workflow needs to be designed allowing users in Lister to pick clothing items using this conveyor.

More on conveyors: https://www.white-conveyors.com/market-dryclean.php

projects.title: Flag Do Not Send Items
projects.description: Designed a manifest-stage feedback loop that flags “do not send” items via fuzzy title matching, helping reduce e-commerce rejection rates without disrupting in-store workflow.
projects.detail: Improved inventory quality for e-commerce by introducing a flagged-items table and confirmation flow during manifest creation, using fuzzy matching against an admin-defined “do not send” list while letting sorters continue their normal process.

sections.heading: Background and Context
sections.content: E-commerce teams were facing a challenges regarding inventory quality and volume. Many of the items being sent to e-commerce from store locations were not meeting the requirements for acceptance in selling online. Despite organizations leveraging functionality to call out items not to send to e-commerce, many items were still being returned to stores and not sold through e-commerce. E-commerce teams have a dependency on store locations to create a strong product flow but lack tools to provide feedback to store team members.

sections.heading: User Stories
sections.content:
Sorter/Manifest Creator

As an in-store sorter and manifest creator who is itemizing products to send to the e-commerce team …

I want to quickly and accurately describe each item and only manifest and send items that are of value for e-commerce …

so I can meet or exceed my accepted rate goals for the month and ensure that my store is contributing positively to the revenue goals of our organization.

sections.heading: Objectives
content: help educate store location teams in sorting and manifests creation on items that are not recommended for selling online
automatically “fuzzy match” manifest item title with the existing keywords outlined in the “do not send list”
make manifest creators aware when a manifested item potentially matches recommendations on a “do not send list”
do not disrupt the manifest workflow and allow manifest creators to continue working as usual even if an item is found to match a “do not send list” item

sections.heading: Hypothesis
sections.content:
We believe that if we create a feedback loop at the manifest creation stage that prevents items being sent to e-commerce …  

will achieve an overall reduction of rejected items from not being sent to e-commerce …

We will know we are successful when the average rejection rate across all organizations drops and the general time to process a manifest is reduced by spending less time annotating rejected products.

Maintain item volume sent from stores

caseStudies.title: Leading Through Ambiguity: AI-Supported Retail Workflows
caseStudies.description: Coached a product designer to lead discovery on a high-risk, sales-driven initiative and stepping in to protect the design team when the research plan stalled unexpectedly.
caseStudies.detail: Coaching a product designer to lead discovery on a high-risk, sales-driven initiative and stepping in to protect the design team when the research plan stalled unexpectedly.

sections.heading: Context
sections.content: This project explored AI-supported workflows to help retail store employees identify products and estimate resale value directly from photos. This capability was already meaningfully impacting customers and their ability to speed up donation processing using the web-based app: pearldive Ama. Seeing a gap in the sales strategy for upselling existing customers using a native app for retail production (Solutions DGR), the Sales team proposed a workflow based on what they believed customers needed: a direct integration between the two systems. Rather than move straight into design, I saw it as an opportunity to test assumptions and ensure we were reducing risk well before development.

content: Identified the need to validate assumptions before committing design or engineering effort
Provided the project framing template used to structure discovery
Coached the project lead through research planning and pivot
Research outreach strategy and messaging
Supported facilitation of the cross-team workshop
Initial discovery, shaping, and framing
Research planning
Led facilitation of the cross-team workshop

sections.heading: Coaching through the first roadblock
sections.content:
Initial project framing was completed by the product designer I manage using the same template I use across all of our projects, documenting the sales team's assumptions clearly enough that we could see how many of them were unverified. In a one-on-one, we discussed research options together and landed on a plan: reach out to existing customers to understand their current product identification and valuation workflows before designing anything new.

The outreach didn't land. Despite a warm handoff from our Customer Experience team, we heard nothing back from our participant pool from the initial ask or the follow-up. We needed to come up with a new plan to maintain momentum.

sections.heading: The pivot
sections.content:
Rather than solve it for her, I used our regular design team sync where myself and two product designers use the space to work through the pivot together. We talked through why customer outreach might be stalling and what alternative paths could still get us reliable signal. The team decided to pivot from external customer interviews to internal team observations and expertise, pulling on what our own Customer Experience and Account Management teams already knew about how customers handled this work today.

From there, I helped the project led curate a cross-team workshop to bring that internal knowledge together and pressure-test the sales team's assumptions directly, but I made a deliberate choice to support facilitation rather than lead it, giving the product designer the room to run the session herself.

sections.heading: Outcomes
sections.content:
Friction Risk Surfaced

The Sales team's proposed workflow was found to be largely misaligned with existing operational workflows for processing incoming donations. Clear patterns emerged within the workshop’s workflow mapping activity showing alignment across organizations on the methods used to sort donated goods and prep them for resale. The existing operational workflows were at odds with the solution outlined by the Sales team

Next Steps

The workshop succeeded in surfacing initial risk and pointed the product team toward exploring alternate directions. Catching this friction risk before any design or engineering work began avoided building toward the wrong solution. The project is now moving forward into design, shaped by what we actually validated rather than what was originally assumed.

sections.heading: Learnings
sections.content: The most important leadership decision in this project wasn't the research pivot, it was choosing not to solve the stalled outreach problem myself. I used this project as a coaching moment to bring the design team together to work through it collectively, and let the product designer led her project.

caseStudies.title: Building a Product Team Operating System from the Ground Up
caseStudies.description: Built a repeatable product investment operating system: framework, planning cadence, and engineering investment reporting, to make prioritization and roadmap decisions transparent across a multi-product Commerce portfolio.

sections.heading: About the company
sections.content: Upright Labs is a B2B SaaS company serving the thrift and secondhand retail industry with web and mobile products for inventory management and e-commerce. After several ownership and organizational changes, the product team now operates within a larger structure while maintaining direct relationships with customers and cross-functional partners in Growth, Customer Experience, and Engineering.

sections.heading: Context
sections.content: I joined Upright Labs in 2022 as the company’s first design hire, assigned to elevate the products and build a design team. Over the next few years I grew into a strategic product team role with additional responsibilities including roadmap planning, customer communications, internal team rollout coordination, and product direction.

sections.subheading: Building a team and a process
sections.content: I hired and began managing a contracted product designer and defined how our team would collaborate, grow, and own their work. In addition to leading the design team, I also led the organization’s first structured roadmap prioritization process and establishing decisions grounded in customer feedback, quantitative data, and a repeatable framework rather than opinions. That framework, and the trust it built with engineering and customer-facing teams, became the foundation I’d later scale across the entire organization.

sections.subheading: Designing for many teams, not just one
sections.content: A sudden organizational consolidation brought several previously independent teams under one shared product function. With the merger of 4 unique businesses and a collective 17 product areas, I began co-owning the combined product function. This became the opportunity to scale the existing framework I’d already proven with one team into a full operating system built for four. Additionally we acquired another product designer and our team grew in size and responsibilities, moving from designers to product owners.

content: Defined guiding principles and company/product priorities as shared evaluation criteria for every initiative, advancing strategy, solving meaningful customer problems, benefiting the greatest number of customers, and protecting platform health

Designed a two-part scoring model: a modified RICE framework (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort) calibrated to our signal sources, paired with a customer-assessment layer (cohort, account health, revenue influence, strategic partnerships)
Defined a four-track project-sizing rubric, from quick wins to strategic initiatives, so scope could be evaluated independently of priority
Mapped the full signal-to-solution lifecycle, from customer feedback and internal signals through discovery, delivery, and measured outcomes
Established a single feedback and feature-request intake form across all product areas and audiences (internal teams and customers) along with weekly triage of incoming requests
Hired and managed a contracted product designer, then 2 contract designers
Owned the consolidated product function with initial support from a product analyst and a technical project manager
Built and launched a release communication site for CX and Growth visibility

sections.heading: The prioritization framework
sections.content:
With several teams now sharing one product function, I evolved my earlier framework into a more rigorous model. Every opportunity, whether a customer request or an internally identified initiative, is evaluated against the same guiding principles before it’s ever scored.

Opportunities that clear that bar are scored two ways: a modified RICE model weighted toward our specific signal sources, and a customer-assessment layer that considers cohort, account health, revenue influence, and strategic partnerships. High-value opportunities with low confidence are routed into discovery before they ever reach the roadmap. I also defined the product goals and created a stable foundation to evaluate initiatives against.

sections.heading: Artifacts and tools
content: Guiding principles and prioritization framework documentation
Process diagram (see below)
Release communications  website for internal teams

sections.heading: Outcomes
content: Built a design team and mentored designers through growth into product owners
Consolidated and standardized product processes
Established a framework for prioritization and roadmap planning
Led the product team through company mergers
Owned product strategy across 17 unique product areas

sections.heading: Learnings
sections.content:
Product leadership at scale is less about owning decisions and more about designing the conditions for good decisions. As my scope expanded from one product team to four businesses and 17 product areas, I learned that a process only scales when people understand and trust the thinking behind it. I focused on making that thinking explicit: what we value, what signals we trust, how we evaluate tradeoffs, where uncertainty should trigger discovery, and how decisions connect back to customer and business outcomes.

As my role shifted from designing products to designing the systems around them, I became more intentional about creating shared language, reducing ambiguity between teams, and making product reasoning visible to people who weren't directly involved in the work. The result was a useful reminder that good product systems should not make an organization more rigid. They should make it more capable, giving teams a consistent foundation while leaving room for judgment, context, and new information.

caseStudies.title: Tools for Reselling Books
caseStudies.description: Led discovery and MVP scoping for a book inventory system serving thrift retailers — translating complex operational constraints into a shippable product strategy that supports multiple workflows without forcing change.
caseStudies.detail: Upright Labs needed a fast, reliable ISBN identification and inventory system for thrift retailers — but workflows varied wildly across organizations (store sorting, warehouse QA, fulfillment). caseStudies.title: Feature: Express List - Redesigning a Core Workflow
caseStudies.description: Reimagined a critical product listing workflow to reduce cognitive load and time-to-list, transforming a long scrolling form into a contextual, card-based interface validated through iterative usability testing.
caseStudies.detail: The existing listing workflow in Upright's web product 'Lister' was a long scrolling form that was difficult to parse and error-prone. Users struggled to identify required fields and complete listings efficiently. I was tasked early in my onboarding to reinvent this critical workflow without disrupting existing users.

sections.content: Upright Labs is a business-to-business SaaS company leading the thrift and secondhand retail industry with web and mobile products for inventory management and e-commerce.

content: reduce the average time-to-list metric across all customer organizations
help users identify fields are needed to configure to create a successful listing
avoid disruption of current workflow
focus user-attention and emphasize required fields
reduce cognitive load for users listing products by reducing the amount of decisions
prevent listing errors from happening by restricting submissions with missing values

sections.content: Take a contextual approach to the listing workflow with a redesigned layout that reduces the amount of content displayed and reduces the amount of data entry necessary for a successful listing. “Express List” was designed to increase the average monthly listings across client organizations and a decrease in the average time-to-list metric while also sustaining the average price per item sold.

The challenges faced by the existing listing workflow were shared with me during my hiring process at Upright. I was tasked early in my onboarding to “reinvent” this critical workflow. Our product team was focused on increasing listing efficiency and reducing the time-to-list metric but was hesitant to disrupt users. This project was handled iteratively and I lead efforts to define objectives and find creative solutions to meeting them. The last phase of work, documented here, encompasses the user interface redesign, user testing, final recommendations based on user feedback, and artifacts generated to facilitate collaboration with the engineering lead assigned to development.

My role

Engineer's role

I created a potential participant recruiting pool using quantitative data based on the amount of custom builder templates an organization uses and varied the participants based on organization size, engagement level, and organization type to create a diverse potential pool of participants.

sections.content: The “Express List” feature is currently in development to finish the front-end implementation and final visual design changes. The workflow is a stronger approach to solving for the original productivity efficiency objective. Iterative design cycles created a layout that is future-proof for planned enhancements and additional features as well as responsive and mobile friendly. “Express List” will be launched to all users upon development completion and will co-exist along side the existing workflow, giving users a choice between the two.

Stepping back into projects with fresh eyes can help to elevate, improve, and strengthen projects with knowledge gained in-between active design cycles.  Working iteratively also helped to redefine and focus the objectives of the project and was necessary to designing holistically.
